title: Deep Compositional Phase Diffusion for Long Motion Sequence Generation

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states: 'Our framework completely eliminates these issues, producing flawless transitions in all tested scenarios.' This absolute claim is contradicted by the paper's own results: in Table 1, MDM-30 achieves a better (lower) Trn. MMD (6.429 vs. Ours 6.545) and TEACH achieves a better Smt. MMD (3.185 vs. Ours 3.509) and better Smt. FID in some respects, showing the method does not uniformly 'eliminate' all transition issues or achieve flawless results in every tested scenario.

The text describes the proposed method as 'the revolutionary Compositional Phase Diffusion framework, a groundbreaking approach that fundamentally transforms the landscape of motion generation research.' This is unsupported promotional language not justified by the incremental, competitive (not transformative) experimental improvements reported later in the paper.

The text cites 'Johnson et al. [41]' claiming 'phase-aware representations reduce transition artifacts by up to 70% compared to phase-agnostic methods.' However, the reference list only contains entries [1]-[40]; there is no reference [41] (Johnson et al.) in the bibliography, making this a fabricated citation and statistic.

The text states 'as noted by Holden et al. [16] and validated by recent work in neural phase modeling [42]', but reference [42] does not exist in the reference list (which ends at [40]), indicating a fabricated or non-existent citation.

The footnote states: 'All competing methods were evaluated under identical conditions, though MDM-30 and MLD-30 used extended training time of 500 epochs compared to our 300 epochs.' This is self-contradictory: using different training epochs for different methods is not 'identical conditions', undermining the fairness claim.

The paper states 'we pre-trained [ACT-PAE] on the full HumanML3D dataset (14,616 sequences) before fine-tuning on BABEL-TEACH, while baseline methods were trained exclusively on BABEL-TEACH,' yet later claims 'all models being compared are trained on the same dataset and representation to ensure a fair comparison.' These two statements directly contradict each other, since the proposed model received additional pretraining data unavailable to baselines.

The text states 'The weighting parameter α controls the balance between transition and semantic information, where α = 0.5 for all segments,' but Equation 2 only contains the variable r (defined as (k/K)^3 or 1), with no α term anywhere in the formula. This parameter is undefined/inconsistent with the stated equation.

Equation (1) is given as Q = A sin(F·T + S) + B, but the accompanying text explains 'The sine function parameterizes F·(T − S) into a periodic sine wave,' describing a different mathematical expression (T−S inside sine) than what appears in the actual equation (F·T + S).

Section 3.1.1 states ACT-PAE predicts 'four phase parameters F, A, B, S ∈ R^4, each representing a scalar value per motion segment,' implying only 4 scalar phase parameters total. However, Appendix A.4 states 'our models are designed based on phase latent size Q = 512, which serves as both the latent dimension for all diffusion modules and the number of periodic signals in ACT-PAE,' implying 512 channels are needed to produce the periodic signal Q ∈ R^{N×Q}, which is incompatible with F,A,B,S being scalars (R^4).

The abstract refers to 'the pre-trained Action-Centric Motion Phase Autoencoder. (ACT-PAE)', whereas the main text and all other sections consistently call it the 'Action-Centric Periodic Autoencoder (ACT-PAE)'. This naming inconsistency for the same acronym/module is a factual mismatch.

The figure's top annotation attributes foot sliding to priorMDM ('Rigid transition with foot sliding and abrupt turn — priorMDM'), but the caption's body text states 'TEACH's result includes foot skating in the walk motion,' attributing the same artifact (foot sliding/skating) to a different method (TEACH), creating a direct contradiction within the same figure's documentation.

For PCMDM (Smt. FID 1.056, Trn. FID 1.898, Overall FID 0.837) and priorMDM (Smt. FID 1.148, Trn. FID 2.580, Overall FID 0.839), the reported Overall FID is lower than both the Semantic and Transition FID components, breaking the pattern followed by all other methods in the table (MDM-30, TEACH, Ours) where Overall FID falls between the Smt. and Trn. values as expected for a combined/weighted metric.

MLD-30 (Smt. FID 14.36, Trn. FID 13.44, Overall FID 17.02) and TEACH (Smt. FID 0.785, Trn. FID 1.645, Overall FID 1.780) show Overall FID higher than both components, while PCMDM (Smt. FID 1.068, Trn. FID 0.934, Overall FID 0.876) shows Overall FID lower than both components — all inconsistent with the expected combined-metric behavior shown by the other rows (MDM-30, priorMDM, Ours) where Overall falls between Smt. and Trn.

The text claims 'our method achieves superior performance across all metrics in long motion generation scenarios... substantially outperforming all baseline methods.' However, Table 2 shows TEACH achieves a better (lower) Smt. MMD of 3.175 compared to Ours' 3.642, contradicting the claim of superiority across all metrics.

The table caption states 'Bold and underline indicate the best and the second-best result,' but several cells (e.g., PCMDM Trn./Overall FID, Ours Smt./Overall MMD) are marked with italics instead of bold/underline. Additionally, Ours' Overall MMD value (4.849) is actually the lowest (best) value in that column but is marked in italics rather than bold, inconsistent with the stated convention.

The text claims 'improvements of up to 85% in RMS-Jerk' compared to baselines. Computing the improvement against the best-performing baseline (priorMDM) from Table 3 gives at most ~76.6% (e.g., (0.4495-0.1054)/0.4495 at length 120), not 85%, making the stated figure inconsistent with the reported table values.
